strengths: The paper proposes a practically appealing amortized approach: UPNet predicts a viewpoint-level uncertainty map directly from an image, avoiding iterative neural-renderer retraining during view selection.
The method is clearly motivated and combines a learned uncertainty predictor with explicit redundancy filtering and temporal aggregation.
Evaluation considers image quality, mesh quality, surface visibility, in-domain and unseen-category settings, and two reconstruction backbones.
The reported inference-time savings are substantial, and several design choices are examined through ablations.
The manuscript is generally readable, with useful pipeline diagrams and uncertainty-map visualizations.
weaknesses: The definition of uncertainty is critically ambiguous. PSNR is higher for better reconstruction, yet the method maximizes the resulting value as uncertainty; the redundancy threshold of 0.1 is also incompatible with raw PSNR. The paper does not specify an inversion or scaling and explicitly says no normalization is used during training or inference, making the core algorithm difficult to reproduce or validate.

The claim that PUN matches the upper bound is not supported by Table 1: for example, ID PSNR is 33.19 versus 36.47 and LPIPS is 0.025 versus 0.017. Moreover, the stated upper bound trains and evaluates on the same 40 views, so it is not a proper novel-view comparison.

Essential controls are missing, including random, uniform, farthest-point, coverage-greedy, and oracle ground-truth-UMap selection. Without these, it is unclear whether gains arise from learned uncertainty rather than simply distributing views over the sphere.

No quantitative evaluation of UPNet itself is provided, such as map error, rank correlation, top-view recall, or selection regret. Only two qualitative examples are shown, preventing assessment of whether the predicted maps meaningfully approximate their targets.

The main and supplementary results appear inconsistent: the default method has PSNR 33.19 in Table 1 but 37.41 in Table S2, with no explanation of a different protocol. Table 3 also omits the upper bound and does not clearly identify whether it uses the ID or OOD split.

Baseline coverage is narrow and excludes relevant learned next-best-view and recent Gaussian-splatting approaches discussed in the paper. PUN also samples a fresh set of 512 candidates each step while baselines use one fixed set, so the selection spaces are not strictly matched.

The 400x efficiency comparison counts online inference but omits NUM generation and UPNet training. This is a valid amortized-computation advantage, but total preprocessing cost, break-even point, model size, and energy cost should be reported.

The evaluation is restricted to centered, normalized synthetic ShapeNet objects, fixed-radius spherical cameras, known object centers, and unconstrained camera motion. Consequently, claims about arbitrary viewpoints, new environments, and practical robotics generalization are overstated.

Statistical support is limited: only three runs are reported, the meaning of their standard deviations is unclear, no significance tests are given, and some claimed improvements over NVF in the ID setting are extremely small.

There are reproducibility and presentation inconsistencies, including an 80/10/10 split in the text versus 90 training instances in Figure S1, an unclear initial-view protocol, insufficient details about background/rendering and mesh extraction, and an incorrect or confusing 3DGS citation to the Nerfstudio reference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical limitation of active view selection: repeatedly fitting a neural representation to score candidate views is computationally expensive.
Amortizing view scoring through a learned uncertainty-map predictor is intuitive, and aggregating predictions from previously acquired views provides an interpretable selection mechanism.
The evaluation considers multiple reconstruction criteria, in-domain and category-held-out settings, two downstream rendering approaches, and several component ablations.

The reported reduction in online selection time is substantial and could be valuable in restricted object-centric settings. weaknesses: The central uncertainty definition is technically ambiguous and potentially directionally incorrect. PSNR is treated as a reconstruction error/uncertainty, yet larger PSNR means better reconstruction. The method maximizes products of these values and applies a threshold of 0.1, while stating that no normalization is used. The paper never specifies an inversion or transformation that would make PSNR behave as uncertainty, so the selection rule cannot be reproduced or validated from the description.

The claimed comparison with an all-views upper bound is misleading. The upper bound is trained and evaluated on the same 40 camera views, whereas other methods train on 20 views and are tested on novel views. This is not a comparable novel-view protocol. Moreover, PUN is not actually close on several metrics: for example, ID PSNR is 33.19 versus 36.47, LPIPS is 0.025 versus 0.017, and visibility is 0.41 versus 0.49.

The claimed superiority over all baselines is weakly supported. In the ID results, the PSNR advantage over NVF is only 0.11 dB while PUN's reported standard deviation is 1.74; SSIM and completion ratio are tied. No paired statistical tests or confidence intervals are provided.

The baseline set omits essential inexpensive controls such as random sampling, farthest-point or spherical-coverage sampling, and fixed uniform trajectories. It also omits the cited supervised and reinforcement-learning next-view predictors. Consequently, it is unclear whether UPNet learns useful object-conditioned uncertainty or merely produces well-spread views on a normalized sphere.

The 400x efficiency claim excludes the substantial offline cost of constructing 62,400 supervision pairs and training UPNet, while comparing against baselines that optimize a representation online for every object. This can still demonstrate an online-speed tradeoff, but it is not an end-to-end computational comparison. Dataset-generation time, energy, and amortization analysis are absent.

The evaluation is narrow: all objects are normalized, centered ShapeNet models observed at one fixed radius with cameras facing the origin. OOD evaluation contains only two held-out categories and 20 objects. This does not substantiate broad generalization to novel categories or arbitrary viewpoints, much less the motivating robotics and large-scene applications.

Important experimental details are inconsistent or missing. The main text specifies 80/10/10 instances per ID category, whereas the supplement describes 90 training instances. The initial view, exact category split, camera-coordinate transformations needed to aggregate local maps, candidate-sampling randomness, NeRF/3DGS configurations, and the scope of Table 3 are insufficiently documented.

The 3DGS gains are unusually large—roughly 6 dB over NVF—but Table 3 lacks an upper bound, budget curves, per-category results, and qualitative reconstructions that could diagnose the result. The cited implementation and 'default parameters' are not sufficient for reproducibility.

The method is technically modest: a pretrained ViT regresses 48 errors produced by a pretrained single-view reconstructor, followed by hand-designed interpolation, thresholding, and multiplication. The paper does not establish that this constitutes uncertainty estimation rather than prediction of one backbone's systematic reconstruction error.

The arbitrary-view claim is overstated. Predictions are defined at only 48 anchors, interpolated locally, and searched over 512 randomly sampled poses on a fixed sphere. Robustness to anchor density, interpolation radius, view budget, threshold choice, product underflow, and non-spherical or variable-distance poses is not evaluated.

strengths: PUN offers a useful and conceptually simple contribution: it amortizes uncertainty estimation with a feedforward predictor, avoiding iterative neural-rendering retraining during view selection.

The reported inference efficiency is compelling: selecting 20 views takes approximately 0.5 minutes versus 175–198 minutes for the evaluated baselines, with substantially lower CPU, GPU, and memory usage.
The evaluation covers complementary image-quality, mesh-quality, and surface-coverage metrics, and includes both NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction backbones.

The method generally improves over the three uncertainty-based AVS baselines. The OOD NeRF improvements are particularly encouraging, including 34.74 versus 33.15 PSNR and 0.78 versus 0.75 visible-area coverage relative to the strongest baseline.
The 62,400-pair Neural Uncertainty Map dataset is potentially valuable, while the predicted maps provide more interpretability than policies that directly output a next view.
The paper includes useful ablations of uncertainty targets, aggregation policies, redundancy filtering, and dataset composition, and evaluates transfer to two held-out object categories.
weaknesses: The claim of performance comparable to the all-view upper bound is overstated. PUN trails it by 3.28 dB PSNR in-domain and 2.17 dB out-of-domain, alongside gaps in LPIPS, MSE, and coverage. Moreover, the upper-bound model is trained and evaluated on the same 40 poses, making it an oracle-like reference rather than a conventional novel-view upper bound.

The definition of PSNR-based uncertainty is technically ambiguous. Higher PSNR means lower reconstruction error, yet the algorithm selects the largest predicted uncertainty and removes values below 0.1. The paper also states that no normalization is used during training or inference. An explicit inversion or transformation is necessary for the method to be reproducible and internally consistent.

The generalization evidence remains narrow: all experiments use centered, normalized ShapeNet objects, known object centers, a fixed radius, clean Blender renderings, and spherical camera motion. OOD testing contains only two categories with ten objects each, so claims concerning arbitrary viewpoints and new environments are too broad.

The baseline suite lacks inexpensive non-learning controls such as random, uniform, or farthest-point spherical sampling, as well as learned next-best-view methods and recent Gaussian-splatting AVS approaches. These comparisons are important for determining whether UPNet is needed rather than a strong geometric coverage heuristic.

Several result statements are inaccurate or insufficiently qualified. PUN does not outperform every baseline on every metric: for example, NVF has higher OOD completion ratio, and several ID metrics are tied. The large run variability for PUN's ID PSNR also makes its small advantage over NVF inconclusive without statistical testing.

The resource comparison excludes the substantial offline cost of constructing NUM and training UPNet. Reporting both amortized inference cost and end-to-end cost would better establish the practical trade-off.

Reproducibility details need improvement: the precise ViT variant is unspecified, the 80/10/10 split described in the text conflicts with the supplement's statement of 90 training instances, Table 3 does not identify its evaluation split, and the ablation PSNR of 37.41 is not reconciled with the main result of 33.19. Code and data are only promised for future release.

strengths: The central idea—amortizing next-view uncertainty prediction with a feedforward network instead of repeatedly fitting a radiance field—is practically motivated and yields a substantial reported reduction in inference time and resource usage.

The paper evaluates selected views with multiple reconstruction backbones and considers held-out instances, held-out categories, lighting changes, camera-distance changes, and limited real-scene data.
The NUM dataset is potentially useful: it contains 62,400 image–uncertainty-map pairs over 13 ShapeNet categories, multiple viewpoints, and four reconstruction-error measures.

The method is clearly presented, and the uncertainty-map visualization provides a reasonably interpretable representation of the selection policy. The paper also includes several component and data-scale ablations.
weaknesses: The uncertainty definition is technically underspecified. PSNR is a similarity measure for which larger values mean lower error, yet the method maximizes the product of quantities called uncertainty. The paper does not explain the required inversion or normalization, although its threshold of 0.1 implies some unreported transformation. It also omits whether angular distances in the exponential interpolation are measured in degrees or radians; these choices radically change the policy and prevent faithful reproduction.

The baseline suite is incomplete and favors the proposed method. PUN uses a large supervised dataset and pretrained models, whereas the main comparisons are costly per-scene NeRF uncertainty procedures. The paper discusses but does not compare against learned or pretrained next-best-view methods such as RL-NBV, Neu-NBV, occupancy-based approaches, or recent Gaussian-splatting methods. Thus the reported 400x speedup largely reflects a difference in problem formulation and offline computation, whose considerable NUM-generation cost is not reported.

Several central claims overstate the results. On NUM-inst, PUN's PSNR advantage over NVF is only 0.11 dB while its reported standard deviation is 1.74 dB, and multiple geometry/coverage results are tied. PUN is also 3.28 dB below the alleged upper bound, so it does not convincingly 'match' it. No paired significance tests or per-object results establish superiority.

The 'upper bound' is not a meaningful view-selection comparison because it trains and evaluates on the same 40 views, while other methods use 20 training views and separate evaluation views. This leakage creates an artificial ceiling and makes the half-as-many-views narrative misleading.

The evaluation on prerecorded real datasets is insufficiently specified. PUN normally selects among 512 arbitrary spherical poses and then requires an image from the selected pose, but MIP360 provides only a finite set of captured cameras. The paper does not explain how candidates are restricted or matched to available images, nor how coordinate frames and spherical assumptions are handled. Only four hand-selected scenes per real dataset are used, further weakening the generalization claim.

Some ablation interpretations contradict the tables. For example, increasing anchors from 12 to 48 improves image-error metrics but worsens accuracy, completion, visibility, and visible area, contrary to the claim of improvement across most metrics. Training with MSE-based maps causes SSIM to fall from 0.990 to 0.870, contradicting the claim that the uncertainty metric has limited impact.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the claimed code/model/dataset URL and reproducibility-statement URL are blank; the ViT variant and several normalization and coordinate-transformation details are missing; dataset splits are inconsistent (8:1:1 in the text versus 90 training instances per category in the supplement); and reported resource values differ between the table and prose.

The method remains limited to centered objects, known camera poses, a fixed-radius unobstructed viewing sphere, and no camera-motion or acquisition costs. These restrictions substantially narrow its relevance to practical active reconstruction and are not resolved by the small real-scene experiment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical limitation of uncertainty-driven active view selection: repeatedly retraining a neural renderer is prohibitively expensive.

Predicting a complete viewpoint-error map with a feedforward network is intuitive, interpretable, and potentially useful; the reported 0.82 correlation with target maps provides some evidence that UPNet learns the intended regression task.
The evaluation considers multiple reconstruction backbones, held-out object categories, lighting and camera-distance changes, and limited experiments on NeRFAssets and MIP360.
The reported inference-time and resource reductions are substantial, and the paper includes several component and dataset-size ablations.
The manuscript is generally readable and visually polished.
weaknesses: The uncertainty definition is technically inconsistent and insufficiently specified. PUN uses PSNR as its default uncertainty target, although higher PSNR means lower reconstruction error, yet it selects the candidate maximizing predicted uncertainty. The manuscript never describes reversing PSNR/SSIM, normalizing targets, or otherwise reconciling their direction with MSE/LPIPS. The 0.1 filtering threshold and multiplicative aggregation also implicitly require a defined scale, but normalization is stated only for visualization. This makes the core algorithm ambiguous and difficult to reproduce.

The supervision target is single-view synthesis error, not the marginal information gain from adding a view to the current multi-view reconstruction. A view may have high prediction error because it is intrinsically difficult, without being especially useful for improving reconstruction. Multiplying independently predicted single-view errors does not establish that the resulting policy approximates conditional information gain, and the paper provides no analysis or oracle-regret experiment validating this central assumption.

The claimed comparison with an “upper bound” is invalid and overstated. That model is trained and evaluated on the same 40 views, so it is not a meaningful novel-view-synthesis upper bound. Moreover, PUN does not match it in the reported results: on NUM-inst it trails by 3.28 dB PSNR and 0.008 LPIPS, while on NUM-cat it trails by 2.17 dB and 0.006 LPIPS. No uncertainty analysis supports equivalence.

Potential data contamination is not addressed. UMap labels are generated with Splatter-Image pretrained on ShapeNet, while both training and evaluation objects are selected from ShapeNet. The paper does not establish that its instances were excluded from Splatter-Image pretraining, undermining claims of instance and category generalization.

Baseline coverage is inadequate for the paper's broad claims. Experiments primarily compare against three iterative NeRF-based methods and uniform sampling, while cited direct prediction, pretrained reconstruction, occupancy-based, reinforcement-learning, and recent Gaussian-splatting active-view methods are omitted. On real-scene datasets, the comparison is reduced to NVF alone.

The experimental protocol is underexplained for MIP360, where arbitrary spherical candidates cannot be rendered as in Blender and only prerecorded camera views exist. It is unclear how candidates are constrained to available images, how selected observations are obtained, and whether all methods receive exactly the same feasible set.

The real-world evidence is too small for the claimed broad generalization: only four selected scenes from each external dataset are averaged, without per-scene results, variability, or statistical tests. NUM-cat likewise contains only two held-out categories.

Several conclusions exceed the tables. PUN does not consistently win all eight metrics: for example, uniform sampling ties or exceeds it on some mesh/coverage measures, and the ablations often show negligible differences or alternative policies winning individual metrics. The manuscript nevertheless presents these results as consistent dominance.

Reproducibility is presently weak: the abstract and reproducibility statement claim that code, models, and datasets are available, but the corresponding links are blank. Important details such as target transformations, candidate sampling seeds, real-scene selection, initialization, and exact baseline configurations are missing.

strengths: PUN presents a clear and practically useful idea: amortizing active-view uncertainty prediction with a feedforward network avoids retraining a neural renderer after every acquisition step.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering unseen instances and categories, altered lighting and camera distance, ShapeNet-derived objects, NeRFAssets, MIP360 scenes, and multiple reconstruction backbones.
The reported efficiency gains are substantial: online viewpoint selection is hundreds of times faster than iterative NeRF-based baselines and uses considerably fewer computational resources.

The paper evaluates image quality, mesh quality, and surface coverage, reports variability over three runs for core experiments, and includes several relevant ablations on uncertainty metrics, selection policies, training-data composition, anchor density, and redundancy thresholds.
The uncertainty maps are interpretable, and the reported correlation between predicted and target maps provides useful evidence that UPNet learns the intended signal.
The manuscript is well organized and visually clear, and it openly states important limitations concerning geometry-aware supervision and the spherical, object-centric camera assumption.
weaknesses: The headline claim that PUN is comparable to or matches the all-view upper bound is overstated. On NUM-inst, for example, PUN obtains 33.19 PSNR versus 36.47 for the upper bound, with similarly material gaps in LPIPS and visibility; substantial gaps also remain on NUM-cat. Moreover, the upper bound trains and evaluates on the same 40 views, making it an idealized data-leaking reference rather than a conventional upper bound under the evaluation protocol.

A central technical detail is underspecified: PSNR is treated as an uncertainty or reconstruction-error value even though larger PSNR means lower error, while view selection maximizes the aggregated value and removes values below 0.1. The paper does not clearly define the inversion and normalization used to turn each metric into a common uncertainty scale. This prevents faithful reproduction and obscures whether the selection equations match the implementation.

The MIP360 protocol is unclear and appears inconsistent with the general experimental description. The method assumes freely sampled object-centered spherical poses rendered in Blender, whereas MIP360 supplies a fixed set of captured cameras and no renderable object model. The manuscript does not explain how candidates are restricted or transformed, how selected observations are obtained, or how the learned coordinate convention applies to these scenes.

Baseline coverage is incomplete in the more realistic evaluations: NeRFAssets and MIP360 compare only against NVF, and recently discussed Gaussian-splatting active-reconstruction methods are not evaluated. Comparisons with learned next-view policies are also absent. This limits support for broad state-of-the-art claims.

The online speed comparison excludes the potentially substantial amortized cost of constructing 62,400 supervision pairs and training UPNet. Reporting inference cost is valuable, but the paper should separately quantify offline data-generation and training costs and qualify the overall compute-efficiency claim.

Several core reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous, including the ViT variant and parameter count, exact UMap preprocessing, baseline training and tuning details, coordinate transformations used when aggregating maps from different current views, and the procedure for sampling valid candidates on real datasets.

Some gains are small or statistically inconclusive. On NUM-inst, PUN improves PSNR only from 33.08 to 33.19 over NVF while having a much larger reported standard deviation, and it ties or trails alternatives on several mesh and coverage metrics. No paired significance or per-instance analysis is provided.

The method remains restricted to isolated, centered objects with known object centers and approximately spherical camera access. Results on only four scenes from each realistic dataset do not yet establish robustness for unconstrained active reconstruction. Overall, the idea is promising, but these protocol and claim-support issues place the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold in its current form.
